html:
An agreement first signed on 6 February 1840 at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands between the British Crown and Māori chiefs. It made New Zealand a British colony and is still seen as the founding document of the country.

The British consul William Hobson drafted the English text quickly, and missionaries translated it into Māori overnight. About forty chiefs signed on the first day, and copies were then taken around the country until over 500 had signed. The two texts do not say the same thing. In English the chiefs gave the Queen sovereignty. In Māori they gave kāwanatanga, governance, while keeping tino rangatiratanga, full chiefly authority, over their lands, villages and treasures.

Settlers and governments soon pushed for land, and the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s and large land seizures followed. The treaty was long ignored by the courts. Māori protest brought it back, and in 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal was set up to hear claims about broken promises. See Māori and New Zealand.
